prize_parts.citation: For the discovery that liquid-liquid phase separation of biomolecules organizes the interior of cells

statement.case_for: Biomolecular phase separation introduced a genuinely new concept of molecular organisation: membraneless compartments such as P granules, nucleoli and stress granules can be understood through phase behaviour, multivalency and interfacial physics. Hyman and Brangwynne showed in 2009 that P granules behave as liquids, and Rosen showed in 2012 with purified components that multivalent interactions are sufficient to drive demixing. The idea has been confirmed independently for more than fifteen years, has reorganised thinking in cell biology and neurodegeneration, and has spawned a physical-chemical toolkit (sequence grammar, saturation concentrations, material-state transitions). It is a physical-chemistry principle that explains a messy biological phenomenon in general terms, which is the kind of discovery I most want the chemistry prize to recognise alongside synthesis and materials.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that debate continues over which cellular condensates are truly phase-separated in vivo and which droplets are in vitro artefacts, so the citation must be written carefully around the principle rather than every claimed function. Credit is also crowded: Pappu and Mittag supplied sequence-grammar and theory that a three-person prize leaves out, and a skeptic could say the field is still maturing. Colleagues may reasonably judge the concept closer to cell biology than to chemistry.

responses.point: Linke ranks perovskites first for clear, quantitative physics and a clear new capability, and ranks condensates third, worried about in vivo relevance and the chemistry-versus-physiology fit.
responses.response: I take the in vivo worry seriously, but the prize-worthy discovery is the physical principle, shown quantitatively with purified components (Rosen) and in living embryos (Hyman, Brangwynne), not the functional status of every candidate condensate. That is the same separation we accept elsewhere, where a mechanism is honoured while its scope is still being mapped. I accept that perovskites are more mature as a technology, but their stability and lead issues and the six-way, contested credit make a clean citation harder than for condensates. I would still want the citation to avoid claiming that all condensates are liquid.

responses.point: Aili puts ionizable lipid nanoparticles first for their pKa-tuned charge-switching design and enormous clinical impact, and notes that the credit among Vancouver, MIT and industry groups is contested.
responses.response: I agree the chemistry is strong and the lipid self-assembly physics is close to my own field, which is why B036 is my first alternative. My hesitation is the one Daniel raises: the decisive ionizable-lipid contribution is spread over at least six people and academia and industry, and the 2023 Medicine prize already honoured the nucleoside modification that made the vaccines work. I would not oppose B036 if the committee can agree on a defensible three, but I do not think we can resolve that attribution from the files in front of us.

responses.point: Zou ranks perovskites first for a clear structure-to-function story and nitrogenase second for atomic-level structure explaining function, while flagging stability and irreproducible early efficiency records.
responses.response: The perovskite structure-to-function story is persuasive, and I share the concern about early hysteresis artefacts, which weakens any narrow priority claim among Miyasaka, Park and Snaith. I would ask whether the committee prefers rewarding a device-efficiency breakthrough while stability is unproven, or a concept like phase separation whose scientific validity has been tested for longer in many systems. On nitrogenase I would ask for the mechanism, not just structure, to be settled before it is prized.

responses.point: Aqvist puts first-principles molecular dynamics (Car and Parrinello) first as a clean two-person, forty-year-old method with overdue recognition, and ranks base editing third.
responses.response: The Car-Parrinello credit is the cleanest on the shortlist and I do not dispute the method's importance or maturity. My qualification is that it is a methods and theory prize in a year when we also have discoveries that changed how chemists and biologists think about molecular organisation, and I would want to see the committee weigh both fairly. Johan's own yardstick of theory-experiment comparison is actually met by condensates too, where binary phase diagrams and measured saturation concentrations are compared quantitatively with polymer-physics theory.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts condensates as a chemistry rather than cell-biology discovery given the in vivo debate.
Whether a three-person cut of Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen can be defended against the claims of Pappu and Mittag.
Whether the ionizable-lipid credit (B036) can be resolved to a defensible three-person group, since I would then reconsider my ranking.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B044. For B036 and B069 my work on lipid self-assembly overlaps scientifically but involves no personal tie to the candidates; I share Lund affiliation with Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, which is not a conflict for any shortlisted candidate.
